section.title: Spiritual Gifts and the Body
section.sectionRationale: The Corinthians prized showy gifts and ranked one another by them, splitting the church into the impressive and the overlooked. Paul answers with a double truth: every genuine gift comes from the one Spirit and is given for the common good, and the church is one body with many different members, each needed, arranged by God Himself. The chapter dismantles both pride and self-pity and prepares for the way of love in chapter 13.
section.thesis: There are many gifts but one Spirit, many members but one body; God gives every gift for the common good and arranges each member as He wills, so that no one may boast and no one may despair, for together the many are the one body of Christ in whom all suffer and rejoice as one.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the confession that Jesus is Lord, made only by the Spirit; the varieties of gifts given by the one Spirit for the common good; the one body of many members, all baptized in one Spirit; and the mutual care of the members, for you are the body of Christ.

units.label: Jesus is Lord, by the Spirit

verses.text: Now about {{pneumatikos|spiritual gifts}}, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed.
You know that when you were pagans, you were influenced and led astray to mute idols.
Therefore I inform you that no one who is speaking by the Spirit of God says, “Jesus be cursed,” and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.
There are different {{charisma|gifts}}, but the same Spirit.
There are different ministries, but the same Lord.
There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people.
Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.
To one there is given through the Spirit the message of wisdom, to another the message of knowledge by the same Spirit,
to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit,
to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues.
All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines.

units.label: One body, many members
units.note: God arranges each part as He wills

verses.text: The {{soma|body}} is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ.
For in one Spirit we were all {{baptizo|baptized}} into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink.
For the body does not consist of one part, but of many.
If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be? If the whole body were an ear, where would the sense of smell be?
But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design.
If they were all one part, where would the body be?
As it is, there are many parts, but one body.

units.label: Members caring for one another
units.note: you are the body of Christ

verses.text: The eye cannot say to the hand, “I do not need you.” Nor can the head say to the feet, “I do not need you.”
On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable,
and the parts we consider less honorable, we treat with greater honor. And our unpresentable parts are treated with special modesty,
whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God has composed the body and has given greater honor to the parts that lacked it,
so that there should be no division in the body, but that its members should have mutual concern for one another.
If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.
Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.
And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues.
Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles?
Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?
But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way.

pneumatikos.gloss: Spiritual things or gifts, that which belongs to and comes from the Holy Spirit. Paul opens the whole discussion with this word, correcting the Corinthians' fascination with the spectacular by anchoring everything spiritual in the Spirit who exalts Jesus as Lord and works for the good of the whole church.

charisma.gloss: A gift of grace, a concrete endowment freely given by God. The word is built on charis, grace, so every gift is unearned and given to serve, not to boast in. There are different charismata but the same Spirit, so variety is His design and no gift ranks a believer above another.

soma.gloss: Body. Paul's master image for the church: one body composed of many different members, each needed, arranged by God. Just as a body is not a single organ but many working together, so the church is diverse by design, and the members belong to one another as one body of Christ.

baptizo.gloss: To baptize, immerse, or plunge. In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body: the same Spirit who unites us to Christ joins every believer, Jew or Greek, slave or free, into the single body. The verb marks entry into the one body and grounds the equality and unity of all its members.

basic.context: The Corinthians treasured the more visible gifts, especially tongues, and used them to rank one another, which only deepened their divisions. Paul redirects them. First, the mark of the Spirit is not spectacle but the confession that Jesus is Lord. Then he shows that the many gifts all come from the one Spirit and are given for the common good, and that the church is one body made of many different members, every one arranged and needed by God. Pride and self-pity both dissolve before this truth.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul is teaching the church how to think about gifts, not simply describing Corinth. His body image is an argument: because the church is one body, diversity is essential and no member is dispensable. He ends by pointing beyond the gifts to the most excellent way, love, which chapter 13 unfolds, so gifts must always be read in the light of love.
basic.originalLanguages: The topic is the pneumatikos, the things of the Spirit. The endowments are charismata, gifts of grace built on the word for grace, so they are given, not earned, and given to serve. Paul's governing picture is the soma, the body: one body of many members. And all are baptizo, baptized, in one Spirit into that one body, so unity and diversity are both the Spirit's design.
basic.typology: Israel was one people made of twelve tribes with different roles; the church is the one body of Christ made of many members with different gifts. As the tabernacle needed many crafts and callings to function, so the body of Christ needs every member. The pattern of one people composed of diverse parts, united by God's presence, finds its fulfillment in the Spirit-indwelt church.
basic.christ: The gifts exist to serve Christ and His body. The Spirit's whole aim is to lead people to confess Jesus is Lord, and the church is not merely like a body but is the body of Christ, so that what is done to the least member is done to Him. Christ is the head who unites and directs the members, and every gift finds its meaning in building up His body.
basic.god: The one God, Father, Son, and Spirit, stands behind the whole chapter: the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God who works all in all. God is the giver who apportions gifts as He determines and the composer who arranges every member as He wills. He honors the parts that lack honor, so that the church reflects His own care for the weak and lowly.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 12 gives a parallel picture of one body with many members and differing gifts. Ephesians 4 shows Christ giving gifts to equip the saints and build up His body. 1 Corinthians 8 names the one God the Father and the one Lord Jesus Christ. 1 Corinthians 13 supplies the most excellent way that crowns the gifts.
basic.oneStory: God has always been forming one people out of many, and now by His Spirit He unites Jew and Greek, slave and free, into the one body of Christ. The variety of gifts is not a threat to unity but its very expression, a foretaste of the new creation where a countless, diverse people worships the Lamb as one. The chapter teaches the church to live now as the one body it truly is.

context.literary:
Chapter 12 is built around a threefold pattern of one and many. It begins with a test, verses 1 to 3, in which Paul sets the confession Jesus is Lord against the curse. It then moves to the source of the gifts in verses 4 to 11, with a triplet: the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God, matched by gifts, ministries and workings. Verse 7 gives the purpose of it all, for the common good, and verse 11 gives the giver, who apportions to each as He determines. The body takes over in verses 12 to 26. Paul states the thesis, one body of many parts, and the body is argued in two directions. In verses 15 to 20 the lesser members are told that they belong, and in verses 21 to 25 the greater members are told that they are needed. The two are balanced like a pair of scales. Verses 27 to 31 apply the picture to the church, with a list of appointments and a series of questions that all expect the answer no, and the chapter ends on a hinge that carries over into chapter 13.

Repetition does much of the work. The word body returns again and again through verses 12 to 27, and the words one and many are heard together over and over. The rhetorical questions of verses 17, 19 and 29 to 30 make the foolishness of uniformity plain. The list in verse 8 to 10 begins and ends with speech, and the list of verse 28 puts tongues last, which matches what Paul is about to say in chapter 14. The final phrase, the most excellent way, points forward and also sets all the gifts beneath it.
context.historical:
Corinth was a city of religious variety and of status. Paul reminds the church in verse 2 that they were once led astray to mute idols, a phrase that echoes the Old Testament mockery of idols that cannot speak, Habakkuk 2:18 and 19 and Psalm 115:5. Pagan worship in a city like this included temples of many gods, and some forms of religion prized trance and ecstatic speech. Many scholars think that the Corinthians, new to the Spirit, were carrying over an expectation that the more dramatic the manifestation, the greater the spiritual standing of the person. Paul answers by giving them a test that no pagan frenzy could meet, which is the confession of the lordship of Jesus.

The picture of the body would have been familiar. Greek and Roman writers often compared a city or a state to a body, and the comparison was commonly used to persuade the lower orders to accept their place under their betters. Paul uses the same picture to say nearly the opposite: the lowly members are indispensable and God has given greater honor to the part that lacked it, verse 24. This was pointed in a church where the rich shamed the poor at the common meal, 11:21 and 22, and where social divisions between slave and free were real, 7:21 to 24. When Paul says that in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, verse 13, he is naming the very lines that divided Corinth. The letter dates to about AD 55, and the gifts it lists belonged to a young church with no inherited structures, which helps explain why order was such an anxiety.
context.canonical:
Chapter 12 draws on a long background of the Spirit's gifts. In Exodus 31:1 to 6 the LORD fills Bezalel with the Spirit for skilled craftsmanship in the tabernacle, so even practical skill is a gift of the Spirit. In Numbers 11:24 to 29 the Spirit rests on seventy elders and then on Eldad and Medad in the camp, and Moses answers a complaint with the wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that He would put His Spirit on them. Joel 2:28 and 29 promises that wish will be granted, and Peter says at Pentecost that it is, Acts 2:16 to 18. John the Baptist says that the Messiah will baptize with the Holy Spirit, Matthew 3:11, and Jesus repeats it, Acts 1:5. Verse 13 is the Christian fulfillment of those promises.

The body image reappears in Romans 12:3 to 8, a shorter parallel that lists gifts and urges sober judgment of oneself, and in Ephesians 4:4 to 16, where Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists and teachers to equip the saints until the body is built up in love. First Peter 4:10 and 11 turns the gift into stewardship, each using what has been received to serve others, and it includes the speech and the service of the congregation. In Colossians 1:18 Christ is the head of the body, which supplies a clause that is missing from this chapter, where the stress falls on the members. The test of verse 3 is repeated in 1 John 4:1 to 3, where the Spirit of God is known by the confession of Jesus Christ come in the flesh.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants his readers to discover something that they have gotten backwards. They believed that the greater the gift, the greater the person, and so they were arguing about rank, with tongues at the top. He takes the whole question away from the person and gives it to the Giver. Gifts come from the Spirit, ministries from the Lord, workings from God, and each is given for the common good. So the very idea of boasting in a gift is shown to be confused, because nobody earned it and nobody owns it.

His second aim is to stop two opposite mistakes that are both ways of leaving the body. The foot who says that he is not a hand and so does not belong is not humble but disloyal. The eye who says to the hand that she is not needed is not strong but blind. Paul writes to both the envious and the proud, and the pairing shows that he is correcting the whole church and not the less gifted or the more gifted alone.

He also means to anchor the matter in the confession of verse 3. The first sign of the Spirit's presence in a person is not the dramatic gift but the plain declaration that Jesus is Lord. This is a corrective to people who thought that spiritual maturity was measured by display. The first hearers were meant to come away with a changed sense of themselves: each is a necessary part, each is given something to give, none can stand alone, and the weakest are honored by God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter's teaching is prescriptive at its center. The Spirit gives to each, the gifts serve the common good, the church is one body and the members need each other, those who seem weaker are indispensable, and there should be no division. These are standing truths for every congregation. The lists of gifts in verses 8 to 10 and 28 are, by contrast, samples. They overlap only partly with the lists in Romans 12 and Ephesians 4, and each list has a different character, which suggests that none of them was meant as a complete catalogue. We should not treat them as a menu of exactly what a church must have.

The order in verse 28 is also not a ranking of persons. Apostles first, prophets second and teachers third describe the foundation of the church's life and the way the gifts of the word serve to build it, Ephesians 2:20. The same verse puts helping and administration among the gifts God has appointed, which reminds us that service and organization are His gifts too, though they are not conspicuous. The questions of verses 29 and 30 do not describe what Corinth had, but what a body could not have: if all were tongue speakers, there would be no body.

The application is practical. Find what you have been given, give it away, do not despise what others have, and do not despise what you have, and do it all in the church's good and not for your own standing.

debates.question: Do the miraculous gifts, such as tongues, prophecy and healing, continue today?

views.label: Continuationist
views.case: Nothing in this chapter says that the gifts will stop before the Lord returns, and Paul says in 13:10 that they pass away when the perfect comes. Verse 28 gives a list of those appointed in the church, and continuationists say that the Spirit still gives all the gifts, for the same purpose of building up the body. They point to Acts 2:17 and 18, which says that the last days are the age of the Spirit's outpouring.

views.label: Cessationist
views.case: Others hold that the sign gifts attested the apostles and the founding of the church, Hebrews 2:3 and 4, and that with the completion of the New Testament they ceased. They point out that the chapter gives a sample of gifts, with no promise about their continuing.

views.label: Open but cautious
views.case: A third view agrees that the Spirit is free to give any gift, yet urges that every claimed gift be tested by Scripture and by the church, 14:29 and 1 Thessalonians 5:19 to 21, and that no gift can be demanded as a mark of a better Christian.

debates.bearing: Paul's own questions in verses 29 and 30 show that no single gift marks every believer, and the whole chapter shows that the gifts exist to serve. Any view that makes a gift a badge of status has already departed from it.

debates.question: What does it mean to be baptized in one Spirit in verse 13?

views.label: The Spirit joins every believer to Christ at conversion
views.case: The sentence says that we were all baptized, past tense and without exception, Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink. A gift said to be given to all cannot be a second experience reserved for some. Many Reformed and evangelical readers hold this view.

views.label: A distinct baptism in the Spirit after conversion
views.case: Pentecostal and charismatic readers connect the phrase with Acts 1:5 and 2:4 and the later experiences of Acts 8, 10 and 19, and read Paul as speaking of the church's general life in the Spirit while holding that a further empowering is both possible and to be sought.

views.label: The Spirit as the agent or the element
views.case: The Greek preposition can mean in or by, so some ask whether the Spirit is the one who baptizes or the one in whom we are plunged. Either way, the result is the one body.

debates.bearing: The context is about unity, and the sentence says one Spirit, one body and all of us. It cannot be used to divide the church into those who have the Spirit and those who do not.

debates.question: What does the command to eagerly desire the greater gifts, verse 31, mean?

views.label: A command to seek the more useful gifts
views.case: The verb can be an imperative, and the greater gifts are those that build up the church most, such as prophecy, which Paul will praise in 14:1 to 5. The command gives permission to ask God for gifts.

views.label: An ironic statement of the Corinthians' habit
views.case: The same form can be a statement, you are eagerly desiring, and some read it as a gentle rebuke of their ambition, followed by a better way. The same root is used of envy in 13:4.

debates.bearing: Both readings put love above the contest, and verse 31 itself ends with a better way. The gifts are good to seek if they are sought for others' sake.

study.originalLanguages:
The triplet of verses 4 to 6 is built from three nouns that overlap and do not exactly divide: charismata, diakoniai and energemata. Gifts of grace, services and workings. Each is attached to a person of the Trinity, Spirit, Lord and God, in an order that anticipates later Christian teaching about the Three, though Paul is not describing the doctrine but observing that one divine work lies behind everything. The word diakonia, service, is the one from which deacon comes, and it reminds us that every gift is a form of waiting on others. Energema, working, comes from the verb energeo in verse 6 and 11, and it is a reminder that God is the one who powers what He gives.

In verse 7 the Spirit's gift is a phanerosis, a manifestation, a showing, and it is given pros to sympheron, for the common good, literally toward what is profitable together. The word sympheron gives the test of every gift: does it bring benefit to the whole? Verse 11 says that the Spirit apportions, from diaireo, to divide out, and does so as He determines, from boulomai, a verb of settled purpose and not of whim. Gifts are distributed by deliberate wisdom.

Verse 13 pairs two verbs, we were baptized, ebaptisthemen, and we were given to drink, epotisthemen, both in the past tense and both with the one Spirit. The second verb is an image of drinking in, which fits John 7:37 to 39, where the Spirit is described as a river of living water. The Greek preposition en can be translated in or by, which feeds the debate noted above.

In verses 18 and 28 God arranged the members, the verb tithemi, to place or set, and he places each one in the body as He wishes. In verse 24 God composed the body, the verb sunkerannumi, to mix or blend together. It is a vivid verb, and it pictures God as one who mixes the colors of a body so that the lowly part gets honor. Paul also plays on words in verses 23 and 24, where the unpresentable parts, aschemona, are treated with special modesty, and in 13:5 the same root appears in the claim that love is not rude, aschemoneo. The body that treats its unpresentable members with care is the one that is shaped by love.

Verse 25 says there should be no division, schisma, which is the word Paul used of the Corinthian cliques in 1:10 and 11:18. So the body argument is the answer to the problem the letter began with. In verse 3 the confession Kyrios Iesous gives to Jesus the title that the Greek Old Testament used for the name of the LORD, which is why Paul can say that no one can make it except by the Spirit.

typology.type: Bezalel and the craftsmen of the tabernacle
typology.fulfillment: In Exodus 31:1 to 6 the LORD fills Bezalel with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship, and gives him Oholiab and other skilled workers. The tabernacle needed many hands, and all of them were Spirit-given. Paul takes that pattern and enlarges it: the church is the true dwelling of God, 1 Corinthians 3:16, built by many members each with a gift. The type is a limited one, since only a few were so named, but in the church the Spirit is given to each, verse 7.

typology.type: The seventy elders and the wish of Moses
typology.fulfillment: When the Spirit came on the seventy elders and then on Eldad and Medad in the camp, Joshua wanted to stop them, and Moses answered, Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, Numbers 11:29. Verses 7 and 13 give the fulfillment. The Spirit is given to each and to all, from the least to the greatest, as Joel 2:28 had said. The type falls short because the elders were a select group, and the Spirit came upon them for a time, while in Christ the Spirit dwells in every believer permanently, John 14:16 and 17.

typology.type: Israel as one people of twelve tribes
typology.fulfillment: Israel was a body made up of different tribes with different roles, camped around the tabernacle, each with its own place. The church is the new people of God, a body in which Jews and Greeks are joined, verse 13, and every member has a place, verse 18. The escalation is that the unity is now by the Spirit and in Christ, and does not depend on birth or land. The type falls short in that Israel's tribal lines were fixed by descent, whereas the body is joined by the Spirit's baptism, which crosses every earlier line.

typology.type: The body as the church, and Christ as its head
typology.fulfillment: Paul says so it is with Christ, verse 12, and you are the body of Christ, verse 27. Later he adds that Christ is the head, Colossians 1:18 and Ephesians 4:15 and 16. The correspondence between a physical body and a community is more than a figure of speech: the church is joined to the risen Christ and acts as His hands and feet in the world. It is not a perfect image, because a human body does not choose its members and cannot be joined by faith, and because Christ is never absorbed into the body but remains its Lord.

study.christ:
Christ stands in the middle of this chapter, though He is named only a few times. The first line of the test is His lordship. No one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit, verse 3. This means that the Spirit's chief work is to point to Him. Jesus said that the Spirit would glorify Him, John 16:14, and here we see the Spirit's work: not first to make people speak in wonders but to bring them to confess that the man from Nazareth is the Lord, which in the Greek Bible is the name of the LORD God. The curse of verse 3, Jesus be cursed, may have come from a pagan or Jewish source, but it shows what is at stake. The confession is that which separates.

Verse 5 names the Lord as the source of the many ministries, which means that the Lord Jesus is the one who assigns the places of service. Ephesians 4:7 and 8 says the same: to each of us grace has been given as Christ apportioned it, and He gave gifts to His people when He ascended. The gifts are the gifts of the risen and exalted Christ, distributed by His Spirit.

The most striking clause is in verse 12: so it is with Christ. Paul does not say so it is with the church. He says that the body, with its many parts, is Christ's, which means that the church is so joined to Him that it can be called by His name. Verse 27 says you are the body of Christ. The truth appears in the way that Jesus asked Saul, why do you persecute Me, Acts 9:4, when Saul was persecuting His people. What is done to the members is done to the head. The Lord's own experience, as one who was weak, dishonored and then given greater honor, Philippians 2:8 and 9, is the pattern of the body Paul describes, where God gives greater honor to the part that lacks it, verse 24.

We should not push the body image into a mechanical allegory in which each member stands for a part of Christ's physical body. The point is the union and the dependence: the church is not a club with Christ as patron but an organism whose life is His. Every gift is a way in which that life flows out to others.
study.god:
The doctrine of God in this chapter is one of its quiet strengths. Paul names the Spirit, the Lord and God in turn, verses 4 to 6, and gives each a part in the same work. It is not a full statement of the Trinity, but it leads to one: the gifts come from the Spirit, the ministries from the Lord, the workings from God, and in each case it is the one God who is at work. The church cannot be understood apart from that unity and that variety, since the God who is behind it is one in being and three in person, and the church's own life, one body with many members, is a creaturely echo of it.

The chapter also shows God as the giver who is sovereign over His gifts. The Spirit apportions to each one as He determines, verse 11, and God has arranged the members of the body according to His design, verse 18. The gifts are not rewards or achievements. They also are not random. This frees the believer from two opposite temptations: the pride that says I earned it and the envy that says I was overlooked. If God has placed me, then my place is not a verdict on my worth.

It shows a God who cares about the weak and the dishonored. In verses 22 to 24 He is the one who has composed the body so that the parts that lacked honor receive more, and the word composed suggests that He does this deliberately and not as an afterthought. That fits the God who is found elsewhere in Scripture taking the side of the poor, the widow and the foreigner, Psalm 68:5 and Deuteronomy 10:18. A congregation that sidelines its quieter members is acting against the character of its Maker.

And it shows God as the one who is present among His people by His Spirit. The Spirit is given to drink, verse 13, so that God is not remote from the church but within it. For worship this means that we should expect God to work through ordinary members, honor those through whom He works, and bring everything back to Jesus as Lord. The goal is the common good, because God Himself seeks the good of the whole body and not the glory of the gifted.

crossReferences.note: A shorter parallel in which Paul tells the Romans not to think of themselves more highly than they ought, then speaks of one body with many members and different gifts. It supplies the same moral lesson of humility and mutual service and lists some gifts that 1 Corinthians 12 does not.

One body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Christ gives gifts to equip the saints so that the body may be built up in love, until it grows into Him who is the head. It is the nearest companion to verses 4 to 6 and 12 to 13.

Each one should use whatever gift he has received to serve others, as faithful stewards of God's grace. It states in other words the point of 1 Corinthians 12:7, that gifts are for the good of others and that God is glorified through them.

The Spirit rests on the seventy elders and on Eldad and Medad, and Moses wishes that all the LORD's people were prophets. This is the Old Testament hope that verse 13 declares fulfilled, with the Spirit given to all God's people.

Bezalel is filled with the Spirit of God for skilled work in the tabernacle. It shows that gifts of the Spirit include crafts and administration as well as speech, which fits the mention of helping and administration in 1 Corinthians 12:28.

God promises to pour out His Spirit on all flesh, including sons, daughters and servants. Peter says that this began at Pentecost. It is the background for the phrase we were all given one Spirit to drink in verse 13, which includes slave and free.

All who are baptized into Christ have clothed themselves with Christ, and there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for all are one. It runs alongside verse 13, with the same list of divisions and the same answer of unity in Christ.

Christ is the head of the body, the church, and in everything He has supremacy. It supplies what 1 Corinthians 12 leaves unstated, that the body has a head, so the unity of the members is the unity of those who are joined to Him.

If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised Him, you will be saved. This confession is the content of 1 Corinthians 12:3 and shows why it is the first mark of the Spirit's work in anyone.

Test the spirits to see whether they are from God, since every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is from God. It shows that the test of verse 3 was not a one-time rule for Corinth but the church's standing way of recognizing the Spirit.

Peter explains Pentecost by quoting Joel: in the last days God will pour out His Spirit on all people, and sons and daughters will prophesy. It places the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 within the new age begun by Christ's resurrection and ascension.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question that the Bible has been asking since Babel. At Babel humanity tried to make a name by unity of its own making, and God scattered the people by confusing their speech, Genesis 11:1 to 9. In Corinth the church speaks in tongues that need interpretation, and Paul is in effect describing the reversal: where Babel scattered, the Spirit gathers. At Pentecost the many languages become a means of hearing the one gospel, Acts 2:5 to 11, and here the many gifts become a means of building one body. The divisions of verse 13, Jew and Greek, slave and free, are the ones the fall produced and the law and the empire hardened, and the Spirit joins what they separated.

Earlier in the story, the Spirit rested on a few. On Bezalel, on the seventy elders, on judges and prophets and kings, the Spirit came for a time and a task. Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets, Numbers 11:29, was left waiting, and Joel promised that it would come, Joel 2:28. Jesus said the Spirit would be with the disciples forever, John 14:16, and the book of Acts shows the Spirit poured out on Jews, Samaritans and Gentiles alike. First Corinthians 12 is a picture of what a people so filled looks like: not a crowd of equals but an organism in which each has something to give.

The passage also looks ahead. Paul says that the gifts are for the present age, and chapter 13 will say that prophecies and tongues will pass away when the perfect comes. Ephesians 4:13 describes the goal as unity in the faith and the full measure of the stature of Christ. In the new creation the body will be complete. No member will be missing and none will be ashamed, for the Lamb's people will stand before the throne from every tribe and language, Revelation 7:9. What the Spirit begins at Pentecost in a few fragile house churches is therefore the beginning of the final gathering, where the honored and the unhonored are one, and the glory that was reserved for few belongs to all.

quiz.q: According to Paul, what is the true test that someone is speaking by the Spirit?

options.text: That they confess Jesus is Lord, which no one can say except by the Holy Spirit.
options.note: Verse 3 makes the lordship of Jesus the mark of the Spirit's work.

options.text: That they display the more spectacular gifts like tongues.
options.note: Spectacle is not the test; Corinth's error was to think so.

options.text: That they feel a strong emotional experience.
options.note: Feelings are not the measure; confessing Jesus as Lord is.

options.text: That they were formerly devoted pagans.
options.note: Their pagan past was precisely what led them astray to mute idols.

quiz.q: Why are there different gifts in the church?

options.text: The one Spirit apportions them as He determines, for the common good.
options.note: Verses 7 and 11: given for the common good by the sovereign Spirit.

options.text: So that the more gifted believers can lead the rest.
options.note: Gifts serve the whole, not personal rank; that was Corinth's mistake.

options.text: Because believers earn different gifts by their devotion.
options.note: They are charismata, gifts of grace, not earned rewards.

options.text: So that each person can pursue his own spiritual benefit.
options.note: They are given for the common good, not private advantage.

quiz.q: What does Paul's image of the body teach about the members?

options.text: There are many different members, each needed and arranged by God, forming one body.
options.note: Verses 18 to 20: God arranges every part; the body is many yet one.

options.text: The stronger members can do without the weaker ones.
options.note: Verse 22 says the weaker parts are indispensable.

options.text: Every member should have the same gift for true unity.
options.note: If all were one part, there would be no body; diversity is the design.

options.text: Members who lack the showy gifts do not really belong.
options.note: The foot and ear still belong; no one is excluded for lacking a gift.

quiz.q: How are believers joined into the one body?

options.text: In one Spirit they were all baptized into one body, whether Jew or Greek, slave or free.
options.note: Verse 13 grounds the unity of the body in the one Spirit.

options.text: By achieving the same level of spiritual maturity.
options.note: Unity rests on the Spirit's work, not on equal maturity.

options.text: By belonging to the same social class or nation.
options.note: Paul deliberately unites Jew and Greek, slave and free.

options.text: By each keeping to their own separate group.
options.note: The Spirit makes the many one body, not many separate groups.

quiz.q: What happens in the body when one member suffers or is honored?

options.text: If one suffers, all suffer; if one is honored, all rejoice together.
options.note: Verse 26 describes the mutual concern of the members.

options.text: The stronger members carry on unaffected.
options.note: That contradicts mutual concern; the whole body is affected.

options.text: Only the leaders need to respond to it.
options.note: Every member shares in the suffering and the joy, not just leaders.

options.text: Nothing, since each member is independent.
options.note: Verse 21 denies that any member can say I do not need you.

questions: Paul says the mark of the Spirit is confessing Jesus is Lord. How does that reframe what you count as evidence of the Spirit at work in someone's life?
Every gift is given for the common good. What gift has God given you, and how are you using it to build up others rather than yourself?
The foot and ear were tempted to feel they did not belong. Where are you tempted to disqualify yourself, or to envy someone else's gift, instead of trusting God's arrangement?
God gives greater honor to the parts that lacked it. Who are the overlooked, weaker members of your church, and how could you honor them this week?
If one part suffers, all suffer. How closely do you actually share in the pain and joy of others in your congregation, and what would deeper mutual concern look like?

translationNotes.note: Spiritual gifts renders the plural pneumatikos, literally the spiritual things; the term can include both the gifts and the people who are spiritual, but here it introduces the whole discussion of Spirit-given endowments.
Gifts translates charismata, gifts of grace built on the word charis; the term stresses that every endowment is freely given by God to serve, never earned or a ground for boasting.
Baptized in one Spirit into one body uses baptizo; the emphasis falls on the Spirit uniting all believers, across every human division, into the single body of Christ.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 1 Corinthians 12:1-31.
